common_name: Buran Pepper (Ukrainian Heirloom Sweet Bull's Horn Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Buran is a Ukrainian heirloom valued for setting fruit early and heavily even where seasons are short.

directions: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after danger of frost has passed. Buran is a compact, early Ukrainian heirloom that sets clusters of tapered, bull's-horn-shaped fruit ripening from pale green to deep red, with thick walls and a sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating or roasting. Its early maturity and heavy fruit set make it a dependable choice for short-season gardens. Pick pods at either the green or fully red stage, harvesting regularly to keep plants producing.

common_name: Chervena Chusha Pepper (Bulgarian Heirloom Sweet Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Chervena Chusha (Bulgarian for red pepper) is a productive heirloom traditionally grown for roasting and preserving.

directions: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55F. Chervena Chusha is a Bulgarian heirloom bearing blocky, tapered fruit with thick, sweet flesh that ripens from green to a deep brick red, a traditional choice in Balkan kitchens for roasting, stuffing, and preserving as ajvar-style spreads. Plants are productive over a long harvest window in hot summer conditions. Harvest some pods green for a milder taste and leave others to fully redden for peak sweetness.

common_name: Giant Szegedi Paprika Pepper (Hungarian Heirloom Drying Paprika)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Giant Szegedi is a long-fruited Hungarian paprika type named for the city of Szeged, historically the center of Hungarian paprika production.

directions: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger passes. Giant Szegedi produces long, tapered, mild sweet fruit that ripens from pale yellow-green to deep red, grown primarily for drying and grinding into traditional sweet Hungarian paprika powder. Plants benefit from a long hot season to bring the full crop to red ripeness for harvest. String ripe pods to air-dry in a warm, airy spot, or use a dehydrator before grinding into powder.

common_name: Yellow Stuffer Pepper (Tomato-Shaped Heirloom Sweet Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Yellow Stuffer is an heirloom named for its squat, tomato-like shape that holds stuffing well without collapsing when baked.

directions: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55F. Yellow Stuffer bears thick-walled, tomato-shaped fruit that ripens from green to golden yellow, bred and selected for sturdy, compact proportions that make it a favorite for whole-pepper stuffing and baking. The dense flesh holds its shape well under heat and has a mild, sweet flavor. Harvest at the yellow stage for the sweetest flavor, or use slightly earlier for a firmer texture.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed; Barattiere is a southern Italian heirloom melon grown for its pale green, smooth-skinned fruit, picked young and used like a cucumber rather than eaten as sweet dessert melon.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, thinning seedlings and giving vines room to sprawl. Barattiere is a traditional southern Italian carosello-type melon, harvested immature at just a few inches long when the pale green flesh is crisp, mild, and cucumber-like rather than sweet. Pick fruit frequently while still young and tender, since the texture coarsens and bitterness can develop if left to mature on the vine. Use fresh in salads or lightly pickled, as is traditional in Puglia and other southern Italian regions.

common_name: Tendral Verde Melon (Spanish Heirloom Winter Melon)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; Tendral is a long-season Spanish winter melon that needs an extended hot summer to ripen and is valued for its exceptional storage life.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep after the last frost once soil has thoroughly warmed, and reduce watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sweetness. Tendral Verde is a traditional Spanish winter melon with smooth, dark green rind and firm, pale green flesh that is mildly sweet rather than intensely aromatic, similar in style to Piel de Sapo but prized above all for its remarkable keeping quality. Properly cured fruit can be stored for weeks to a few months in a cool, dry place, which historically made it a valued melon for eating well past the end of the growing season. Harvest when the rind dulls and the blossom end yields slightly to gentle pressure.

common_name: TAM Uvalde Melon (Texas A&M Open-Pollinated Cantaloupe)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; TAM Uvalde is an open-pollinated cantaloupe developed by Texas A&M for better tolerance of powdery mildew in hot, humid growing regions.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained hills once frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest plants. TAM Uvalde is an open-pollinated cantaloupe bred at Texas A&M for improved resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem for melons grown through hot, humid summers. It produces medium-sized, heavily netted fruit with sweet, salmon-orange flesh typical of Western cantaloupe types. Keep soil evenly moist during vine growth and fruit sizing, then ease off watering as melons near ripeness, harvesting at full slip when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed; Krymka is a Crimean heirloom melon valued for ripening in regions with a shorter or cooler summer than classic Western cantaloupes need.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest seedlings and giving vines room to sprawl. Krymka is a Crimean heirloom melon bearing smooth to lightly netted, pale green-skinned fruit with aromatic, sweet, pale green to cream-colored flesh, grown across Eastern Europe in gardens with shorter or less reliably hot summers than classic American cantaloupe regions require. Keep soil evenly moist while vines establish and fruit develops, then reduce watering as melons approach ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the fruit develops a strong sweet fragrance at the blossom end and yields slightly to gentle pressure.
